entry: [[Pseudoscience|Pseudoscientific]] historical race concept that emerged in the late 19th century, holding that the descendants of the [[Proto-Indo-Europeans]] formed a racial grouping. The term derives from Aryan, a self-designation of Indo-Iranians meaning "noble." Anthropological, historical and archaeological evidence does not support the concept. Racist and antisemitic writers, including [[Richard Wagner]], adopted it, and by the 1930s it was linked to [[Nazism]] and used to support a "master race" ideology. In [[Nazi Germany]] these ideas formed part of the state ideology that led to the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]].

Dried gum oleoresin exuded from the rhizome or taproot of several Ferula species. The resin is produced in [[Iran]], [[Afghanistan]], India, Central Asia and northwestern China. It is used mainly in Indian and Middle Eastern cuisines to complement or substitute for [[Garlic|garlic]] and [[Onion|onion]], though its strong odor has limited its use in the West. It has been used in [[Ayurveda|Ayurvedic]] and Western herbal medicine, particularly for gastrointestinal and respiratory complaints. Since 2020, India has undertaken efforts to establish domestic cultivation, notably in [[Himachal Pradesh]].

Former Akan state in present-day [[Ghana|Ghana]], 1701–1902. Established in the late 17th century by King Osei Tutu and his adviser Okomfo Anokye, with the Golden Stool as its unifying symbol, it expanded under a reorganized army. In 1701 it conquered Denkyira, gaining access to the [[Gulf of Guinea]] and to coastal trade with Europeans, notably the Dutch, on the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. Its economy rested on gold and agricultural exports, as well as slave trading and trade with markets further north. The Asante defeated the British in the first two of five Anglo-Ashanti Wars and killed army general Sir Charles MacCarthy in 1824, but British forces later burned the capital, [[Kumasi]]. After the fifth war the empire became part of the Gold Coast colony on January 1, 1902. Today the Asante Kingdom survives as a constitutionally protected, sub-national traditional state within Ghana, and its current king is Otumfuo Osei Tutu II.

Group of six naturally occurring fibrous silicate minerals that is toxic and [[Carcinogen|carcinogenic]]. Asbestos has been used for at least 4,500 years, when people in the Lake Juojärvi region of [[Finland|East Finland]] strengthened pottery with it. Large-scale mining began at the end of the 19th century, and for much of the 20th century asbestos was widely used as a fire-retardant building material until its health effects were more widely recognized in the 1970s. Inhaled fibers can cause [[Mesothelioma|mesothelioma]], asbestosis and [[Lung cancer|lung cancer]], typically after a latency period of about 20 years. Asbestos is completely banned in 66 countries and strictly regulated in many others, yet around 255,000 people are thought to die each year from asbestos-related diseases. Russia, the top producer, produced an estimated 790,000 tonnes in 2020.

Volcanic island in the South Atlantic Ocean, part of the British Overseas Territory of [[Saint Helena|Saint Helena]]. Discovered by the Portuguese seafarer João da Nova in 1501 and named by [[Afonso de Albuquerque]] in 1503, it was garrisoned by the British Admiralty from October 22, 1815, to 1922. It was an important naval and air station in [[World War II]] and a staging point during the [[Falklands War]]. The island hosts RAF Ascension Island, a [[European Space Agency]] rocket tracking station and a ground antenna for the [[Global Positioning System]].

Lifestyle of abstinence from worldly pleasures, often pursued for spiritual goals. Ascetics renounce material possessions and physical pleasures, live simply, and often fast while concentrating on religion, prayer or meditation. The practice has been observed in ancient Greek schools such as [[Stoicism]] and in [[Buddhism]], [[Hinduism]], [[Jainism]], [[Christianity]] and [[Islam]]. Ascetics maintain that self-imposed constraints bring greater clarity of thought and the ability to resist destructive temptations. The adjective derives from the Greek áskēsis, meaning "training" or "exercise."

Phylum of fungi, known as sac fungi or ascomycetes, and the largest phylum of fungi. Together with [[Basidiomycota]] it forms the subkingdom Dikarya. Its defining feature is the ascus, a microscopic sexual structure in which nonmotile ascospores form, although some species are asexual. Familiar members include morels, [[Truffle|truffles]], brewers' and bakers' [[Yeast|yeast]], and the fungal partners of most [[Lichen|lichens]]. Ascomycetes ferment bread, alcoholic beverages and cheese, and produce [[Antibiotic|antibiotics]]. Many are [[Pathogen|pathogens]] of animals, including humans, and of plants, causing diseases such as apple scab, rice blast and powdery mildews. Species of [[Cordyceps]] parasitize and kill insects, and [[Model organism|model organisms]] such as Neurospora crassa and Aspergillus species are used in genetics research.

Reproduction without the fusion of gametes or change in chromosome number. Offspring inherit the full set of genes of a single parent and are genetically identical to it, or clones. Asexual reproduction is the primary form of reproduction for single-celled organisms such as [[Archaea|archaea]] and [[Bacteria|bacteria]], which divide by binary [[Fission (biology)|fission]]. Some cells divide by budding, as baker's yeast does, and hydras reproduce by budding. Plants reproduce vegetatively, for example through [[Strawberry|strawberry]] runners and [[Tulip|tulip]] bulbs. In vertebrates the most common form is [[Parthenogenesis|parthenogenesis]], and some monitor lizards, including [[Komodo dragon|Komodo dragons]], can reproduce asexually. Asexual reproduction is fast and needs no mate, but it produces limited genetic diversity, which leaves populations vulnerable to environmental change, disease or predators.

Lack of sexual attraction to others, or low or absent interest in sexual activity. Asexuality may be considered a [[Sexual orientation|sexual orientation]], or the lack of one, and is distinct from [[Celibacy|celibacy]] and sexual abstinence, which are generally motivated by personal, social or religious beliefs. The term also covers a range of identities called the ace spectrum. Some asexual people engage in sexual activity to please a partner or to have children, and some form romantic or nonsexual partnerships. Researchers disagree on whether asexuality is an orientation, and asexual individuals may represent about one percent of the population. The Asexual Visibility and Education Network, founded in 2001 by David Jay, is the most prominent of the asexual communities that formed after the mid-1990s.

Capital and largest city of [[Turkmenistan]] (pop., 2022: 1,030,063). Founded in 1881 on the basis of an Ahal Teke tribal village, it became capital of the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic in 1924. A 1948 earthquake destroyed much of the city, which was later rebuilt under the "White City" urban renewal project of Saparmyrat Nyýazow, with monumental buildings sheathed in costly [[Marble|white marble]]. The Soviet-era Karakum Canal carries water from the [[Amu Darya]] through the city, which lies between the [[Karakum Desert]] and the Köpetdag mountains.

King of the [[Neo-Assyrian Empire]], 669–631 BC. He inherited the throne as the favored heir of his father, Esarhaddon, and his 38-year reign was among the longest of any Assyrian king. His campaigns against [[Elam]] defeated it in a series of conflicts in 665, 653 and 647–646. His brother Shamash-shum-ukin, relegated to vassal status in Babylonia, rebelled in 652 and died during the siege of [[Babylon]] in 648. A patron of art and literature, Ashurbanipal built a library at [[Nineveh]] that perhaps held over 100,000 texts at its height, a collection not surpassed until the [[Library of Alexandria]]. More than 30,000 [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] texts have survived. He is also recognized as one of the most brutal Assyrian kings, and his destruction of Elam has been described as a [[Genocide|genocide]].

Inter-governmental forum of 21 member economies around the Pacific Rim, headquartered in [[Singapore]]. Founded in 1989 in response to the growing interdependence of Asia-Pacific economies, it followed the success of [[ASEAN|ASEAN]]'s post-ministerial conferences. Leaders of member economies attend an annual Economic Leaders' Meeting, where they traditionally wear the national costume of the host country. The 1994 Bogor Goals targeted free and open trade by 2010 for industrialized economies and 2020 for developing ones, but those deadlines were not met. Critics argue that its non-binding structure limits its effectiveness.

Continental multi-sport event held every four years for athletes of Asia, also known as Asiad. Recognized by the International Olympic Committee, the Games are the second-largest multi-sport event after the [[Olympic Games]]. The first edition was held in [[New Delhi]] in 1951. The Asian Games Federation regulated the Games until 1978; since 1982 they have been organized by the Olympic Council of Asia. Nine nations have hosted the Games, and 46 nations have participated, including Israel, which was excluded after its last participation in 1974. In 1962 Indonesia refused to permit Israel and Taiwan to take part, and the IOC terminated its sponsorship. Since 2010 hosts have commonly staged the Asian Para Games shortly afterward. The twentieth edition was scheduled for Aichi Prefecture and [[Nagoya]], Japan, from September 19 to October 4, 2026.

Medium-sized Asian bear adapted to life in trees. It is distributed from southeastern Iran and the [[Himalayas]] to mainland Southeast Asia, Korea, China, the Russian Far East and the Japanese islands of Honshū and [[Shikoku]]. It has 74 [[Chromosome|chromosomes]]. Its closest relative is the [[American black bear]], from which it is thought to have diverged about 3 million years ago, though genetic evidence is inconclusive. Listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, it is threatened by [[Deforestation|deforestation]] and by poaching for body parts used in [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]].

Second-largest living elephant and the only living species in the genus Elephas. Adult males average 4 t (4.4 short tons). It is found from [[India]] and [[Nepal]] to [[Borneo]] and [[Sumatra]], and eats about 150 kg (330 lb) of vegetation a day. It is highly intelligent and self-aware, displaying behaviors associated with grief, learning and greeting. Listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List since 1986, it is threatened by habitat loss, fragmentation and poaching, and its population has declined by at least 50% over three elephant generations.

World's largest hornet, native to East, South and mainland Southeast Asia. Also known as the northern giant hornet, it prefers low mountains and forests, feeding mainly on larger insects, other social insects, tree sap and [[Honey bee|honey bee]] colonies. Its 6 mm stinger injects a large amount of potent [[Venom|venom]]. Briefly found in the [[Pacific Northwest]] from late 2019, it was eradicated there by December 2024. In 2022 the Entomological Society of America said it would adopt the name northern giant hornet to avoid potentially discriminatory language.

Large monitor lizard of South and Southeast Asia, widely considered the second-largest lizard after the [[Komodo dragon]]. It has a natural affinity for water and inhabits lakes, rivers, swamps, [[Mangrove|mangroves]] and urban waterways. An excellent swimmer, it hunts fish, frogs, invertebrates and water birds. Adults rarely exceed 1.5–2 m (4 ft 11 in – 6 ft 7 in), but the largest specimen on record, from [[Sri Lanka]], measured 3.21 m (10.5 ft). Listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List because its population appears large and stable.

Lion subspecies (Panthera leo leo) whose surviving population is restricted to [[Gujarat]], India. Adult males weigh about 160 kg (350 lb). Until the 19th century the lion ranged across [[West Asia]] to central India. Since the early 20th century its range has been limited to Gir National Park and surrounding areas. The population rose from 411 individuals in 2010 to 674 in 2023 and an estimated 891 in 2025. The Asiatic lion is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List.

First ruler of the Askia dynasty of the [[Songhai Empire]], reigning 1493–1528. Born Muhammad Ture, he was a prominent general under Sunni Ali. He challenged the succession of Sunni Ali's son Sunni Baru on the grounds that Baru was not a faithful Muslim, and defeated him in 1493. Under his rule the empire reached its greatest extent, including the Hausa states as far as [[Kano (city)|Kano]]. He standardized trade measures, policed trade routes, organized a tax system and instituted a bureaucratic government. His policies expanded trade with [[Europe]] and [[Asia]], created many schools and established [[Islam]] as an integral part of the empire. He was overthrown by his son, Askia Musa, in 1528.

Capital and most populous city of [[Eritrea]], at an elevation of 2,325 m (7,628 ft). Asmara became the capital of Italian Eritrea in 1897, after Italy occupied it in 1889. Under Italian [[Colonization|colonial]] rule it grew rapidly and was called *Piccola Roma* ("Little Rome"). Its Italian colonial modernist architecture led [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] to designate it a [[World Heritage Site]] in 2017. The 1939 census recorded 98,000 people, 53,000 of them Italian. More than 400 buildings are of Italian origin, and many shops still have Italian names. Local tradition holds that the city was founded when four villages united to end long periods of conflict.

Perennial [[Flowering plant|flowering plant]] native to Eurasia, widely cultivated for its young shoots, which are used as a spring vegetable. Once classified in the [[Liliaceae|lily family]], it is now placed in the Asparagaceae. The plant grows typically to 100–150 cm (3–5 ft) tall, with needle-like cladodes and bell-shaped flowers that are usually dioecious. Its fruit is a small red berry that is toxic to humans. Since asparagus often originates in maritime habitats, it thrives in soils too saline for normal weeds. Crowns are planted in winter, and the first shoots appear in spring; the first pickings, called sprue, have thin stems. In 2024 world production was 8.9 million [[Tonne|tonnes]], led by China with 87% of the total.

Former diagnostic category of [[Autism|autism]], marked by difficulties in social interaction and nonverbal communication and by restricted, repetitive behavior and interests. Named in 1976 by psychiatrist Lorna Wing after Austrian pediatrician Hans Asperger, who described such children in 1944, it was merged into autism spectrum disorder in the DSM-5 (2013) and ICD-11 (2022). In 2015 it was estimated to affect 37.2 million people, about 0.5% of the population. Edith Sheffer's 2018 book *Asperger's Children* claimed that Asperger was complicit in the Nazis' murder of disabled children.

Deficient supply of oxygen to the body arising from abnormal breathing, causing generalized [[Hypoxia (medicine)|hypoxia]] that can lead to [[Coma|coma]] or death. Causes include airway obstruction from [[Asthma|asthma]] or foreign material, low-oxygen environments such as underwater or a vacuum, and chemical exposure. Carbon monoxide binds to [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]] more tenaciously than oxygen does, displacing it, and [[Hydrogen cyanide]] is another hazard. In 2015 about 9.8 million cases of unintentional suffocation occurred, resulting in 35,600 deaths. The word derives from [[Ancient Greek|Ancient Greek]] roots meaning "without" and "squeeze."

Genericized trademark for acetylsalicylic acid, a [[Analgesic|nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug]] (NSAID) used to reduce pain, fever and [[Inflammation|inflammation]]. Aspirin is also an antithrombotic, used long term to reduce the chance of [[Myocardial infarction|heart attack]], ischemic [[Stroke|stroke]] and blood clots in people at high risk. Its common side effects include an upset stomach, and serious ones include stomach ulcers, bleeding and worsening [[Asthma|asthma]]. It is not recommended in the last part of pregnancy or generally for children with viral infections, because of the risk of Reye syndrome. Its precursor, salicin from [[Willow|willow]] bark, has been used for at least 2,400 years. Felix Hoffmann of Bayer, or perhaps Arthur Eichengrün, first produced acetylsalicylic acid in pure, stable form in 1897.

State in [[Northeast India|northeastern India]], in the [[Brahmaputra River|Brahmaputra]] and Barak River valleys. It covers 78,438 sq km (30,285 sq mi) and shares international borders with [[Bhutan]] and [[Bangladesh]]. The 2011 census recorded 31.2 million people. Dispur is the capital, and [[Guwahati]] is the largest city. The state is known for Assam tea and Assam silk. [[Kaziranga National Park|Kaziranga]] and Manas National Parks are [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Sites]], and more than half of the extant wild population of the one-horned Indian rhinoceros lives in the state.
